source: Sarkar p181-210, p356-390, p506-515; RangDale9 ch8, ch16; Katzung16 appendix 2

cards.front: Classify: the four scales of measurement
cards.text: {{Nominal}} data are labels without order (e.g. sex, hair colour; a two-category nominal variable is dichotomous); {{ordinal}} data are ranked but the gaps are unknown (e.g. satisfaction scores, visual analogue scale); {{interval}} data have equal known gaps but no true zero (e.g. temperature in Celsius); {{ratio}} data have equal gaps and a true zero (e.g. weight, height).

cards.front: Which summary measures can be used on each scale of data?
cards.back: Nominal: mode only. Ordinal: mode or median, not the mean, because ranks cannot be added. Interval: mode, median, mean and SD (addition and subtraction allowed, ratios not, since there is no true zero). Ratio: all of these plus ratios and the coefficient of variation. Interval and ratio data suit parametric tests; nominal and ordinal data need non-parametric tests.

cards.front: Distinguish discrete from continuous, and qualitative from quantitative data.
cards.back: Continuous variables can take any value on a scale and be subdivided indefinitely (e.g. temperature, litres of fuel); discrete variables take fixed countable values (e.g. number of heads in 100 tosses). Quantitative data are measured numerically and can be computed; qualitative data describe attributes (e.g. honesty, creativity) that are observed but not calculated.

cards.front: Define mean, median and mode. When is the median the better summary?
cards.back: Mean: sum of values divided by their number. Median: middle value of ordered data (average of the two middle values when n is even). Mode: most frequent value. The median is better when outliers are present, e.g. for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10,000 the mean is 2002 but the median is 3. In a normal distribution mean, median and mode are equal and half the values lie on each side of the mean.

cards.front: What is standard deviation and how is it calculated?
cards.back: A measure of how widely values are spread around the mean; a small SD means values cluster near the mean. Steps: find the mean; find each deviation from it; square and sum the deviations; divide by n - 1 to get the variance; take the square root. In a normal distribution, mean plus or minus 1 SD covers about 68% and plus or minus 2 SD about 95% of values. SD is also used to derive the standard error and to plan sample size.

cards.front: Why is the sample variance divided by n - 1 rather than n?
cards.back: Dividing by n - 1 makes the sample variance an unbiased estimate of the population variance: averaged over all possible samples it equals the population value, whereas dividing by n underestimates it.

cards.front: Distinguish standard deviation from standard error of the mean.
cards.back: SD describes the spread of individual observations in one sample. The standard error of the mean (SEM) is the SD of the sampling distribution of means, i.e. how much sample means scatter around the population mean. SEM = SD divided by the square root of n, so it shrinks as sample size grows.

cards.front: Which pairs of central value and spread does a results section use?
cards.back: Mean with standard deviation or standard error, or median with interquartile range.

cards.front: Short note: Standard error and confidence limits

points: Used to determine confidence limits, in Student's t test and in analysis of variance
Increasing the number of observations reduces the margin of error

cards.front: Define prevalence. How do point and period prevalence differ?
cards.back: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time: all existing cases (old and new) divided by the population. It is cross-sectional. Point prevalence uses the population at one moment; period prevalence uses the average or mid-period population over a defined interval and is mainly used for chronic disease, insurance and hospital statistics.

cards.front: Distinguish incidence proportion (cumulative incidence) from incidence rate (incidence density).
cards.back: Both count only new cases. Incidence proportion = new cases during a stated period divided by the number initially at risk; it is a risk (0 to 1), needs a closed cohort and a stated follow-up time. Incidence rate = new cases divided by person-time at risk (e.g. per 1000 person-years); it is a rate (0 to infinity) and can be measured in an open population.

cards.front: What is an odds ratio, how is it calculated and interpreted?
cards.back: The odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls; from a 2x2 table (a, b = exposed cases, controls; c, d = unexposed cases, controls), OR = (a/c)/(b/d) = ad/bc. It is the measure of association in case-control studies. OR = 1: no association; above 1: exposure linked to the outcome; below 1: possibly protective. It needs no population denominator, but association does not prove causation.

cards.front: What is relative risk and from which study design is it obtained?
cards.back: Risk of the outcome in the exposed divided by risk in the unexposed: [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]. It needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies, not case-control studies. RR = 1: no effect; above 1: exposure raises risk; below 1: exposure lowers risk. It is a descriptive measure and does not by itself test significance.

cards.front: Complete: when the odds ratio approximates relative risk
cards.text: In case-control and cohort studies the odds ratio approximates the relative risk when the outcome occurs in less than {{10%}} of the unexposed (i.e. a {{rare}} outcome); when the outcome is commoner, the OR {{overestimates}} the RR.

cards.front: What is the number needed to treat (NNT), and why is it more informative than relative risk reduction?
cards.back: The number of patients who must be treated for one more patient to benefit (or be harmed) in a defined way. It is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, so it depends on baseline risk and is more informative than a relative risk alone.

cards.front: Essay: Choosing the measure of association and effect size for case-control, cohort and trial data

points: Odds ratio ad/bc; approximates RR only if outcome <10% in non-exposed, else overestimates
Incidence known in both groups, so relative risk directly
NNT depends on baseline risk: 50% to 25% mortality gives 4; 5% to 2.5% gives 40
Show NNT for benefit and harm side by side
Association is not causation

cards.front: What is a P value, and how are P values conventionally interpreted?
cards.back: The probability, calculated from the test statistic, of getting the observed result if the null hypothesis were true. It is compared with a significance level (alpha) chosen in advance, usually 5% (also 1% or 0.1%); P below alpha leads to rejecting the null hypothesis. Rough guide: P > 0.10 no evidence against the null; 0.05-0.10 weak; 0.01-0.05 moderate; 0.001-0.01 strong; < 0.001 very strong.

cards.front: Distinguish the null hypothesis, alternative hypothesis and research hypothesis.
cards.back: Null hypothesis (H0): no difference between a sample and the population, or between samples; it can be rejected but never proved. Alternative hypothesis (H1): there is a difference (greater, smaller or simply different). Research hypothesis: a specific, clear, predictive and testable statement about the expected outcome based on background knowledge.

cards.front: Short note: Steps of hypothesis testing

points: State H0 and H1
Data type, sample size, sampling technique, distribution of data
Significance level alpha, usually 5%
Shows how many standard errors the sample result lies from the value stated in H0
P <= 0.05: reject H0 (significant)
P > 0.05: retain H0

cards.front: What does a 95% confidence interval mean, and why is it reported alongside the P value?
cards.back: For a large sample, mean plus or minus 1.96 SE gives a range expected to contain the population mean in 95% of samples; values outside it would occur by chance only 5% of the time. Unlike a P value alone, a CI shows the direction and size of the effect and its precision. In a forest plot a study whose CI crosses the line of no effect is not statistically significant.

cards.front: Short note: Possible decisions in hypothesis testing

points: Correct decision (probability 1 - alpha)
Type I error, false positive (alpha)
Type II error, false negative (beta)
Correct decision; probability 1 - beta = power
Use as large a random sample as possible; pre-specify the significance level

cards.front: How does sample size affect the standard error of the mean?
cards.back: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n, so it falls as the sample grows. The variance of the sampling distribution of the mean is the population variance divided by n, so larger samples give means that cluster more tightly around the population mean.

cards.front: What power is usually accepted for a clinical trial, and why?
cards.back: Power of 0.8 to 0.9, an 80-90% chance of detecting a real effect, is often acceptable. Type II errors are regarded more leniently than type I errors, and a larger sample size gives greater power.

cards.front: In the Rang and Dale example, how many subjects are needed to detect a fall in mortality from 50% to 40%?
cards.back: About 850 subjects, at p < 0.05 with a power of 0.9.

cards.front: How does trial size change the smallest relative risk a trial can detect?
cards.back: For the same control event rate, a larger trial can detect a smaller relative risk. Rarer outcomes need a larger relative risk to be detected at the same trial size.

cards.front: Short note: Null hypothesis

points: The hypothesis usually set up in practice: there is no difference between the groups compared
Tests are built to see whether the data allow rejection of this null hypothesis

cards.front: When is the t test used instead of the Z test, and what are its requirements?
cards.back: Both test whether two means differ more than chance allows. For small samples (n < 30) Z values do not follow the normal distribution, so Student's t test (W.S. Gosset, pen-name "Student") is used, with probability read from the t table at the right degrees of freedom. Requirements: random sample, quantitative data, normally distributed variable.

cards.front: Classify: types of t test
cards.text: The {{unpaired}} (independent) t test compares means of two separate groups, df = {{n1 + n2 - 2}}; the {{paired}} t test compares before-and-after values in the same subjects, df = {{n - 1}}; the {{one-sample}} t test compares a sample mean with a known or hypothesised population mean.

cards.front: Classify: types of ANOVA
cards.text: {{One-way}} ANOVA tests one factor with three or more levels; {{two-way}} ANOVA tests two factors and their interaction (equal numbers per cell needed); {{factorial}} ANOVA (e.g. 2x2 design) studies several factors and their interactions in one experiment; {{repeated measures}} ANOVA compares related means, e.g. the same patients at three time points, extending the paired t test.

cards.front: Classify: non-parametric counterparts of parametric tests
cards.text: Two independent groups: {{Mann-Whitney}} test (for the independent-measures t test); more than two independent groups: {{Kruskal-Wallis}} test (for one-way ANOVA); two repeated conditions: {{Wilcoxon}} test (for the matched-pair t test); more than two repeated conditions: {{Friedman's}} test (for repeated-measures ANOVA).

cards.front: Classify: correlation tests
When is ANOVA used, what are its assumptions, and what statistic does it give?
cards.back: To compare means of more than two groups, where repeated t tests become unreliable (for two groups it gives the same result as the t test). Assumptions: each group from a normal population, equal variances, independent samples, random independent observations. It splits total sum of squares into between- and within-group parts and gives the F ratio (between-group mean square divided by within-group mean square), read from the F table.

cards.front: Short note: Chi-square test

points: Non-parametric test for categorical (frequency) data; developed by Karl Pearson
Test of proportion: compare incidence of an event between groups
Test of association (independence) between two attributes
Goodness of fit: observed vs expected distribution
Build a contingency table of observed frequencies (O)
Derive expected frequencies (E) from row and column totals; compare O with E cell by cell and sum
df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1); compare with table value at chosen alpha
Unreliable if any expected value in a 2x2 table is < 5 (or > 20% of cells in larger tables); Yates correction for 2x2 only
Shows association, not its strength or causation

cards.front: Compare parametric and non-parametric tests.
cards.back: Parametric tests assume a normal distribution, equal variances, interval or ratio data and independence, and use the mean; they have more power. Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests suit ordinal or nominal data, small samples or non-normal data, use the median and resist outliers, but have lower power, so type II error is more likely. Data that violate normality should be analysed non-parametrically.

cards.front: Short note: Student's t-test

points: Parametric test: applied when the data are assumed to be normally distributed
Compares the means of two samples: the difference between means is divided by the standard error of that difference
Null hypothesis: no difference between the two means

cards.front: Short note: Non-parametric tests

points: Distribution-free methods, used when normal distribution cannot be assumed
Increasingly popular for analysis of biological data

cards.front: Essay: Choosing and applying tests of significance in a drug study

points: H0, H1; alpha fixed beforehand
Nominal/ordinal vs interval/ratio; normality; paired or independent
Z test (large n) or t test: unpaired, paired, one-sample
ANOVA: one-way, two-way, factorial, repeated measures
Chi-square: proportion, association, goodness of fit
Non-parametric tests; lower power
P value with 95% CI; type I and II errors; power

cards.front: Define meta-analysis and outline how one is done.
cards.back: Statistical analysis of results from many studies to integrate their findings (Glass, 1976); a quantitative alternative to a narrative review. Steps: frame the question as PICO(T); search databases and grey literature (e.g. MEDLINE, EMBASE, theses, congress abstracts); screen abstracts and full papers against inclusion criteria; extract data and assess study quality; compute effect sizes; examine their spread and moderators; interpret and report.

cards.front: What is evidence-based medicine (EBM), and how is the evidence obtained?
cards.back: Using the best available research evidence, after critical appraisal, together with the doctor's clinical skill and the patient's preferences to make care decisions. It aims to improve outcomes, reduce harm, improve cost-effectiveness and support shared decisions. Evidence is found by literature search (e.g. the TRIP database) and synthesised by systematic reviews and meta-analysis.

cards.front: Classify: reporting guidelines by study type
cards.text: {{CONSORT}} for randomised trials (25-item checklist plus flow diagram); {{PRISMA}} for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (27 items); {{STROBE}} for observational cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies (22 items); {{MOOSE}} for meta-analyses of observational studies; {{STARD}} for diagnostic accuracy studies; {{SPIRIT}} for trial protocols.

cards.front: What are the strengths and weaknesses of meta-analysis?
cards.back: Strengths: greater power and precision from pooled data, resolves conflicting trials, quantifies inconsistency, allows subgroup analysis, and pooled RCTs give the highest level of evidence. Weaknesses: selective reporting and publication bias (negative studies are less often published), double counting of the same data, heterogeneity of populations, time-consuming search and complex statistics.

cards.front: Short note: Reading a forest plot

points: Horizontal: effect measure (OR, RR, risk difference, SMD)
Vertical line of no effect: 1 for ratios, 0 for differences
Box = point estimate; box size = study weight (size)
Horizontal line = 95% CI; crossing the no-effect line = not significant
Diamond: centre = pooled estimate, width = its 95% CI; touching the no-effect line = overall result not significant

cards.front: What does a Kaplan-Meier plot show in the rizatriptan example?
cards.back: The probability of relief from migraine pain, plotted against hours after dosing, for 10 mg rizatriptan and for placebo, so the two groups can be compared over time.

cards.front: Why are rare drug toxicities usually missed before marketing?
cards.back: Some toxicities occur in about 1 in 10,000 patients or fewer, and several hundred thousand patients may need exposure before the first case appears. Trials are too small to detect them, so such effects usually surface only in phase 4, after marketing.

cards.front: Short note: CONSORT statement

Reduces bias by making trial reports complete and transparent
Failure to follow it is linked to rejection of papers by international journals

points: Pools data from similarly conducted randomized controlled trials of the same drug or class with the same end point
Larger numbers raise significance and power

cards.front: Short note: Evidence-based medicine

points: Systematically finding, evaluating and using current research as the basis of clinical decisions
From experience-based (impression of the physician) to decisions guided by credible evidence from well designed trials

cards.front: Classify: methods of random allocation and sampling
cards.text: Methods include {{simple}} (lottery or random numbers), {{systematic}} (every kth unit), {{stratified}} (random within homogeneous strata), {{multistage}} (random at successive levels, e.g. district then village), {{cluster}} (natural groups such as villages), {{multiphase}} (sub-samples of a sample), {{block}} (equal numbers per block), unequal and {{minimisation}}.

cards.front: What does randomisation achieve, and what are the criteria of a good method?
cards.back: It removes selection bias (with allocation concealment), balances known and unknown covariates between arms, and provides the basis for statistical tests. A good method is unpredictable (each participant has the same chance of any arm), produces balanced groups, and is simple to use.

cards.front: What inputs set the sample size of a study?
cards.back: Research question, study design, expected effect size, significance level, statistical power, unit of analysis and analytical approach.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Sample size determination across study designs in health professions education research: a methodology guide F1000Res 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13562950

cards.front: Is there one universal sample-size formula?
cards.back: No. Requirements depend on the design and inputs, so formulas are design-specific.
refs: WEB EuropePMC Sample size determination across study designs in health professions education research: a methodology guide F1000Res 2026 https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13562950

cards.front: Complete: Z values in sample-size formulas
cards.text: For a two-sided α of 0.05, Zα/2 = {{1.96}}; for α of 0.01, Zα/2 = {{2.58}}. For 80% power, Zβ = {{0.84}}; for 90% power, Zβ = {{1.28}}.

cards.front: How do block randomisation and minimisation keep groups balanced?
cards.back: Block randomisation assigns equal numbers to each arm within small blocks (e.g. AABB, ABAB in blocks of 4), so groups stay equal in size even if the trial stops early; with fixed blocks, staff may predict the next allocation. Minimisation assigns each new patient to the arm that best reduces imbalance in key factors (e.g. sex, age, disease stage) and suits very small trials (about 50 patients).

cards.front: How is cluster sampling used to estimate immunisation coverage?
cards.back: Natural groups such as villages are listed with their populations; 30 clusters are chosen systematically by a sampling interval and random start. In each, houses are surveyed from a random first house until 7 eligible children are found, giving 210 children. Cluster sampling is cheaper and quicker but has higher sampling error and may miss diversity.

cards.front: Short note: Types of control groups in clinical trials

points: Identical dummy; measures absolute efficacy; ethically limited when effective treatment prevents serious harm
Used when blinding is not feasible; cannot be blinded
Randomised to fixed doses, may include placebo; blinding easier to keep
Standard treatment; fewer ethical problems; needs sound reason to expect the new drug is at least as good
Patients outside the trial; all get the new drug; prone to bias, no randomisation or blinding
e.g. active plus placebo; helps when the active control's efficacy is uncertain

cards.front: Where must a trial report state its sample size calculation, and what can an inadequate calculation cause?
cards.back: It must be clearly defined in the methods section, and protocol review checks the statistical methodology including the sample size calculation. An inadequate calculation can lead to false-negative results.

cards.back: 63 per group.

cards.front: Short note: sample size

points: A key design decision that determines whether real effects can be detected
Per-group closed-form formulas use Z values for significance level and power
Underpowered studies miss real effects
Overpowered studies waste participants and resources
State effect size and assumptions, not a single bare number

cards.front: Short note: Sample-size formulas for comparing two groups

points: n = 2 (Zα/2 + Zβ)² σ² / d²
σ = standard deviation of the outcome; d = smallest clinically important difference in means
p1, p2 = expected proportions in the two groups
Zα/2: standard normal value for the significance level (1.96 for two-sided α = 0.05)
Zβ: value for power (0.84 for 80%, 1.28 for 90%)
Effect size: difference to detect; standardised effect = d / σ
Inflate for expected dropouts: n / (1 − dropout rate)
Formulas differ by design; use the one matching the study

cards.front: How does each input change the required sample size?
cards.back: Larger SD raises n (n rises with σ²). Smaller difference to detect raises n (n rises with 1/d², so halving d quadruples n). Stricter significance level (smaller α) raises n. Higher power raises n. A one-sided test needs fewer subjects than a two-sided test. Expected dropouts require a larger starting sample.

cards.front: Give the sample-size formula for estimating a single proportion (prevalence).
cards.back: n = Z² p (1 − p) / L², where Z = 1.96 for 95% confidence, p = expected prevalence and L = allowable absolute error (precision).

cards.front: Why is a post hoc power calculation uninformative?
cards.back: It is done after data collection and adds nothing beyond the p-value.

cards.front: Define the coefficient of variation and say when it is used.
cards.back: Relative spread: the standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage (CV = SD / mean x 100). It lets you compare variability between data sets with different units or scales.

cards.front: How is the coefficient of variation used in planning a study?
cards.back: Preliminary results give the mean and SD, so the CV can estimate sample size with n = t^2 x CV^2 (t for the chosen probability, CV as a fraction). It also compares the variability of two measurement methods.

cards.front: What is a Type I error?
cards.back: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). Its probability is the significance level alpha, usually 0.05; p < 0.05 means a false positive is less than 1 in 20.

cards.front: What is a Type II error, and what is the power of a trial?
cards.back: Type II error: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative), with probability beta. Power = 1 - beta, the chance of detecting a real difference; trials are often designed for power of 0.8 to 0.9.

Enzyme on the well surface reacts with a substrate to form a colour
Activity read against standards of known concentration gives a standard curve
Detection and quantification of specific antigens or antibodies in biomedical research
Quality control in industry
Digoxin measurement in serum

cards.front: Short note: Detecting and evaluating chemically induced liver injury

points: Overt toxicity: clinical signs, macroscopic and microscopic lesions
Surrogate markers: serum liver enzyme levels
Exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects
Liver homogenates are assayed for lipid peroxidation (malondialdehyde, TBARS), reduced glutathione and catalase in antioxidant screening models
Combine markers with histology; use the findings to set the no-observed-adverse-effect level

cards.front: Essay: Statistical methods to determine sample size

points: Smallest number of subjects that is ethically and financially sound
Decided in advance, in the protocol
Significance level (type I error), usually 0.05
Power, usually 0.8 to 0.9 (type II error = 1 - power)
Magnitude of the clinically important difference
Variability (SD or CV) from preliminary data
n = t^2 x CV^2 for the chosen probability, using preliminary mean and SD
Power and difference change the required n: smaller differences need more subjects
State the reasons for the sample size, the power, the significance level and the analysis plan
Adjust for expected drop-outs
An inadequate sample risks a missed effect or a false claim

cards.front: Give the formula for the impact factor of a journal.
cards.back: IF = citations received in one year / papers published in the previous two years, counting original papers, reviews and similar articles.

cards.front: Essay: Impact factor, its calculation, use and misuse

points: Eugene Garfield introduced it in the 1950s
Measures the average citations per article of a journal over a time window
Citations in the year to articles published in the two previous years, divided by the number of those articles
Helps authors choose a journal with high citation frequency
High-IF journals such as the NEJM, Lancet and JAMA are read by both physicians and researchers
Average citation says little about one article
Garfield intended it to manage library journal collections
Misuse: judging scientists or grant decisions, which the inventor never intended
Use impact factor to compare journals, not to rank individual researchers

cards.front: What does the biostatistics team do in a clinical trial?
cards.back: It analyses the data as set out in the protocol and decides whether the study was positive or negative. It also prepares statistical tables, figures and graphs with their interpretation for the medical writers.

cards.front: Essay: Role of the biostatistician in clinical research

points: Member of the trial team, working from the protocol
Helps plan the design, sample size and analysis plan
Specifies the outcomes and the handling of missing data
Analyses the data as per protocol
Tests the hypotheses and reports whether the result is positive or negative
Prepares tables, figures, graphs and their interpretation for the medical writers
Statisticians are outnumbered; a team should not skip statistical input and rely on intuition
The biostatistician makes the trial's conclusions defensible

cards.front: Essay: Sampling and its various types

points: Sampling selects a subset of a population so that results can be generalised
The method depends on population size, homogeneity and the sampling frame
Simple random: every unit equally likely; chosen unit by unit
Systematic: sampling interval K = population / desired sample; random start, then every Kth unit
Stratified: population split into strata; sample drawn in proportion to each stratum
Cluster: natural groups (village, ward, school) chosen at random; cheaper, but higher sampling error
Multistage: random selection at successive levels (district, taluka, village)
Multiphase: all screened, subsample tested further
Systematic needs a complete list of the population
Cluster suits large, scattered populations such as immunisation surveys
A representative sample improves external validity

cards.front: What is cluster sampling, and what is its main disadvantage?
cards.back: Whole natural groups such as villages, wards or schools are chosen at random and surveyed in full. It is cheaper than sampling individuals, but it commonly has higher sampling error.

cards.front: Short note: Volume of distribution and its clinical significance

points: Apparent volume into which a drug seems to distribute: amount in body / plasma concentration
Example from the book: 1000 mg giving 50 mg/L gives 20 L
Lipid to water partition coefficient, pKa, and plasma protein binding
Small V (e.g. warfarin) means the drug stays in plasma
Large V (e.g. digoxin) means most drug is in tissues, so haemodialysis removes little
Pathological states such as heart failure, uraemia and cirrhosis change V
Loading dose depends on V and F, not on clearance

cards.front: Define apparent volume of distribution.
cards.back: The volume a drug would have to fill to produce its observed plasma concentration, V = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is a proportionality constant, not a real fluid volume.

cards.front: Essay: Imperfect data analysis and its remedies

points: Missing data from drop-outs or lost follow-up
Outliers and animal deaths
Inclusion and exclusion criteria that change results
Multiplicity in statistical testing
Missing follow-up can hide serious adverse events
Negative trials left unpublished exaggerate the benefit of new drugs
Plan prospectively how missing data and outliers will be handled
Report and discuss missing data, outliers and animal deaths with the results
Pre-specify the analysis and avoid changing it after data are seen
Honest reporting of imperfect data is part of valid appraisal

cards.front: Short note: Preclinical drug disposition studies

points: Preclinical development includes pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and toxicology
Done in vitro and in animals before first human dosing
No-observed-adverse-effect level from overt toxicity, surrogate markers and exaggerated pharmacodynamic effects
Human equivalent dose obtained from animal dose on a body-surface-area basis
Data variability and bias in interpretation
Multiplicity in statistical testing, inadequately addressed

cards.front: Short note: Pragmatic trials

points: Shows whether an intervention works in routine practice, including its good and bad consequences
Lax inclusion criteria and a heterogeneous population, as seen in daily practice
Active or usual-care control and flexible dosing
Analysis restricted to those who actually received the intervention
Explanatory trials use strict criteria, placebo and fixed dose to show how an intervention works
Pragmatic trials with usual care as comparator are increasing in number

cards.front: Compare explanatory and pragmatic trials.
cards.back: An explanatory trial uses a strict, homogeneous population, placebo and fixed doses to test whether and how an intervention works. A pragmatic trial uses real-world criteria and flexible practice to test how it works in routine care.

cards.front: What is the principle of essentiality in medical research?
cards.back: Research should use human subjects only when this is absolutely essential and no other alternative is available. It is one of the ten core principles of the Indian GCP guidelines.

cards.front: Why does missing data matter in a clinical trial?
cards.back: Participants who drop out, often because the drug did not help, leave gaps in the outcomes. Important events such as serious adverse effects may then go undetected, so the handling of missing data must be planned in advance.

cards.front: Adverse drug reaction vs adverse event: how do they differ?
cards.back: Adverse drug reaction (ADR): a noxious, unintended and undesired drug effect at doses used in humans; it requires treatment, a dose change or caution with future use, and trivial effects are excluded. Adverse event: any untoward medical occurrence during treatment that need not be caused by the drug. Causality is assessed afterwards.

cards.front: Precision vs accuracy: how do they differ?
cards.back: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other (reproducibility). Readings can be precise but inaccurate, for example tightly clustered values all away from the true value.

cards.front: What is stratified randomisation?
cards.back: Subjects are first grouped into strata by a key factor such as age, sex or disease severity, and then randomly allocated within each stratum. This keeps that factor balanced between arms, which matters most when the groups are small.

cards.front: Distinguish randomisation from stratification in a trial.
cards.back: Randomisation allocates every subject to a study arm by chance. Stratification first sorts subjects into strata by a known factor, and allocation within each stratum is still random.
